title: Moshoeshoe Spares His Grandfather's Killers
text:
In the 1820s southern Africa was torn by the wars and migrations known as the Lifaqane, or Difaqane. Whole communities were scattered, crops were destroyed, and some starving groups turned to cannibalism. In 1824 Moshoeshoe, a young Basotho chief, led his people to the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu, which became his stronghold. On the way, his aged grandfather Peete was captured by a band of cannibals and eaten.

Moshoeshoe's followers wanted revenge. The French missionary Eugene Casalis, who lived among the Basotho from 1833 and knew Moshoeshoe well, reported what the chief decided instead. When the cannibals were in his power, Moshoeshoe refused to kill them. He gave them cattle and land so they could live by farming and herding rather than by eating people. According to the tradition, he said they had become the living graves of his grandfather, and he would not disturb a grave.

Former enemies and refugees of many origins settled under his protection. From these scattered people Moshoeshoe built the Basotho nation, which became the kingdom of Lesotho, and he is honored there as its founder.
lesson: Mercy toward people who have done terrible harm can sometimes accomplish what revenge cannot. Turning enemies into neighbors is how lasting peace is built.
source: Eugene Casalis, The Basutos (1861); later Basotho oral histories
caveat: The chief's exact words and some details come from oral tradition recorded years later.
